text: Every real dataset has holes. A customer skips a form field, a system fails to record a value, or a join finds no matching row. In T-SQL these holes are NULL; in pandas they show up as NaN, or None in text columns. This lesson shows how to measure them, understand them, and decide what to do about them — in exactly that order.

Here's a small, illustrative customer table — eight made-up rows with a customer id, a city, an age, and a monthly spend. A couple of cities are missing, a couple of ages are missing, and a couple of spend values are missing too — scattered deliberately so we have real gaps to work with.

Isna returns True wherever a value is missing. Because True counts as 1, sum counts the gaps per column — city, age, and monthly underscore spend each show 2 missing. Mean gives you the share instead — round it, and all three columns sit at 0.25, a quarter missing.

To see the actual rows behind those numbers, use the isna result as a filter — customers where age is na — the same idea as where age is null in SQL. That pulls back customer 102 and customer 105, both missing an age.

Data people describe three broad situations. Missing by chance — gaps random and unrelated to anything else, where dropping them rarely biases your results. Missing by pattern — the gap depends on another column; group by whether age is missing and compare monthly spend, and customers with no recorded age average 137.75, versus 238.75 for everyone else. That's a real pattern, and filling blindly would hide it. And missing means something — a blank cancel date might just mean the customer is still active, where the gap itself is information, not an error.

Dropna removes rows. Drop only where monthly underscore spend is missing, using subset, and you keep six of eight rows. Drop any row with any gap at all, with no subset, and you keep only three — more than half the data gone. Always name the columns that actually matter with subset, and check exactly how many rows you lost before you commit to dropping.

Fillna replaces gaps with a value — but flag what you filled first. Set age underscore missing to the isna result before you touch anything, then fill age with its own median, 39.5, and fill city with the label Unknown. The median is a good default for numbers with a few extreme values; a label like Unknown keeps a text gap explicit instead of making it invisible.

For a smarter fill, use each row's own group — fill monthly underscore spend with the median spend for that customer's city, computed with groupby and transform. One gotcha worth knowing: a row with no city belongs to no group at all, so its monthly underscore spend stays NaN even after this fill. Fills only work when the grouping column itself is present, so fill the group key first if you need every row covered.

To recap: isna dot sum and isna dot mean measure missing data, and filtering on isna shows you the actual rows. Diagnose the reason before choosing a fix. Dropna with subset removes rows; fillna replaces gaps with a value. And always flag filled values, recording what you did, so the analysis stays honest.
